title: Scale for one heavy query—or for many waiting queries
goal: Separate query-size capacity from query-concurrency capacity, then make the choice in Databricks and Snowflake.
concept:
Imagine a supermarket. A wider checkout lane helps one shopper with a huge cart. Opening more lanes helps many shoppers who are waiting. Data warehouses have the same two controls: make a worker larger for a heavy query, or add workers/clusters for concurrency.

Do not resize first and ask why later. Look at the symptom: one query spills or runs slowly, or many otherwise healthy queries sit in a queue.
example: At 09:00, one finance query needs 70 capacity units. At 10:00, twelve dashboard queries each need 10. A 40-unit worker cannot run the finance query efficiently; a single 80-unit worker can. But twelve dashboard requests still queue behind one another unless the service can add clusters.

use_case.when: Use this decision whenever a SQL endpoint is slow: first distinguish per-query pressure from concurrency pressure.
use_case.example: A month-end reconciliation spills on one cluster, while the morning BI dashboard is fast once it starts but waits in a queue.
use_case.decision: Scale up for a query that cannot fit or parallelize well. Scale out for many independent queries waiting. Add auto-stop/suspend only after choosing the right capacity shape.

practice: Move the heavy-query size and concurrent-query count. The diagram changes from a wider lane to more lanes and explains the bottleneck.
boundary: The browser uses synthetic capacity units and a simple queue formula. Real engines schedule stages, cache data, isolate workloads, and charge differently. The Databricks and Snowflake SQL below is unexecuted vendor practice.
js:
function paintCapacity(){const need=+heavyNeed.value,n=+queryCount.value,size=need>40?80:40,clusters=n>4?Math.ceil(n/4):1,wait=Math.max(0,n-clusters*4);capacityWorld.innerHTML='
Heavy query
'+need+' units needed
Scale up
worker capacity '+size+'
Arrivals
'+n+' small queries
Scale out
'+clusters+' lanes · '+wait+' initially waiting

Reason: worker size answers “can one query run well?”; cluster count answers “how many can start together?”

';}heavyNeed.oninput=paintCapacity;queryCount.oninput=paintCapacity;paintCapacity();
questions: One query spills while there is no queue. First capacity move?
The symptom is one query exceeding its lane, not many queries waiting.
Queries are fast after they start, but twenty wait. Best direction?
More lanes address waiting independent work.
Idle-time controls address cost, not query semantics.

steps.note: Start with a heavy query that exceeds one worker shape.
Choose a larger shape for the single-query need.
Now model many independent dashboard queries.
Add lanes until all twelve can begin in this teaching model.

walkthrough.limit: The browser uses synthetic capacity units and a simple queue formula. Real engines schedule stages, cache data, isolate workloads, and charge differently. The Databricks and Snowflake SQL below is unexecuted vendor practice.

visual_explanation: Read the diagram as two separate questions. The left pair compares one query with one worker. The right pair compares arrivals with available lanes; it never suggests that a larger lane automatically creates more lanes.
written_questions: Which production metrics would distinguish spill/scan pressure from queue pressure?
Where would you isolate dashboard and ETL workloads instead of scaling one shared endpoint?

product_sections.title: Snowflake: warehouse size versus multi-cluster concurrency
product_sections.html:
Use case. A reporting warehouse must run a large reconciliation and absorb a dashboard burst.

Unexecuted vendor SQL. Run only with change control. The browser visual is local JavaScript.

ALTER WAREHOUSE reporting SET WAREHOUSE_SIZE = LARGE;ALTER WAREHOUSE reporting SET  MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT = 1 MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT = 4  SCALING_POLICY = STANDARD AUTO_SUSPEND = 600;

Failure/fix. Resizing changes the resources of each cluster. Multi-cluster adds clusters for concurrency and requires the relevant Snowflake edition. Auto-suspend/resume controls idle use; verify caching and latency effects before shortening it.

title: A savepoint can undo the optional step—not the whole order
goal: Use a database savepoint when one optional operation may fail inside a larger transaction.
concept:
A cashier rings up an order, then tries to apply optional loyalty points. If the loyalty step fails, you may want to keep the valid order rather than throw away the whole basket. A savepoint is a bookmark inside the transaction: roll back work after the bookmark, then continue.

In PostgreSQL, an error leaves the transaction unable to continue until you roll back to a savepoint (or roll back the transaction).
example: The order insert succeeds. The loyalty insert violates a constraint. ROLLBACK TO loyalty_step removes only the loyalty work and clears the error state. The order can still commit, provided that this degraded outcome is allowed by the business contract.

use_case.when: Use a savepoint when a multi-step database transaction has an explicitly optional sub-step and all work lives in the same transactional database.
use_case.example: Persist an order even when an optional loyalty-credit write fails, then enqueue a repair record inside the same transaction.
use_case.decision: Use a savepoint only when partial success is a valid business state. Roll back everything when the failed step is required for correctness, money movement, or invariants.

practice: Choose where the failure happens and step through the transaction timeline. Watch which rows survive.
boundary: The local model is not a database and does not model locks, isolation, JDBC driver behavior, nested savepoints, or external services. A savepoint cannot atomically undo a Kafka publish or HTTP call.
js:
function paintSave(){const f=saveFail.value,rows=f==='required'?[]:f==='optional'?['order 42','repair marker']:['order 42','loyalty +10'];saveWorld.innerHTML='
Required order
'+(f==='required'?'FAIL → full rollback':'saved')+'
Savepoint
'+(f==='optional'?'ROLLBACK TO marker':'not needed')+'
Commit contains
'+(rows.join('
')||'nothing')+'
';}saveFail.onchange=paintSave;paintSave();
questions: After an optional PostgreSQL statement errors, what enables the transaction to continue?
Rolling back to the savepoint restores the transaction state before the optional step.
When should the whole transaction roll back?
A cosmetic audit field failed and degradation is approved
A savepoint has a short name
Required business invariants must remain atomic.
Can a database savepoint undo an already-sent HTTP request?
The savepoint controls work in that database transaction, not external side effects.

steps.note: The required order write succeeds.
Bookmark the transaction, then attempt optional work.
Simulate the error and ROLLBACK TO the bookmark.
Record the degraded outcome and commit the still-valid transaction.

walkthrough.limit: The local model is not a database and does not model locks, isolation, JDBC driver behavior, nested savepoints, or external services. A savepoint cannot atomically undo a Kafka publish or HTTP call.

visual_explanation: The required order sits before the bookmark. Only work to the right of the bookmark is erased. If the required order fails, the picture deliberately removes every committed row.
written_questions: Which optional database step in your service has a documented degraded outcome?
What external side effect would make a savepoint unsafe here?

title: Show unit cost before you charge teams
goal: Turn shared-platform spend into a decision metric without hiding unallocated cost.
concept:
A restaurant bill is not useful for improvement until you know what was ordered. Likewise, “the data platform cost $420k” does not say whether efficiency improved while usage doubled. Pair cost with a business output, such as successful terabytes processed.

Showback makes costs visible. Chargeback bills teams. Start with showback while tags and shared-cost allocation are still being repaired.
example: Team A costs $12,000 and successfully processes 600 TB: $20/TB. Team B costs $8,000 for 200 TB: $40/TB. Another $5,000 is unallocated. Do not smear that unknown cost across teams and call it precise; publish the gap and fix ownership.

use_case.when: Use unit-cost showback when a shared platform must connect engineering choices to business output.
use_case.example: Compare monthly Spark platform cost per successful terabyte by domain, while exposing untagged shared services separately.
use_case.decision: Move toward chargeback only when ownership, allocation rules, dispute paths, and unit definitions are stable enough that teams can act on the numbers.

practice: Change Team B output and unallocated cost. Watch total spend stay the same while decision quality changes.
boundary: The model assumes one synthetic unit and simple direct allocation. Real programs need amortization, commitments, shared services, failed work, data-quality rules, and anti-gaming controls.
js:
function paintCost(){const b=+teamBTb.value,u=+unknownCost.value,total=12000+8000+u;costWorld.innerHTML='
Team A
$20/TB
Team B
$'+(8000/b).toFixed(0)+'/TB
Unallocated
$'+u+'

Total $'+total+'. Unallocated cost is shown, not silently reassigned.

';}teamBTb.oninput=paintCost;unknownCost.oninput=paintCost;paintCost();
questions: Why pair cost with successful TB?
To connect spend with useful output
A unit metric shows efficiency as workload volume changes.
What should happen to unallocated cost?
Visible uncertainty creates a repair target without false precision.
Allocation rules are unstable and disputed
Billing on weak attribution creates distrust and bad incentives.

steps.note: Start with allocated spend and successful output.
Compute comparable unit costs.
Keep unknown shared cost visible.
Measure confidence in the showback before using it as a bill.

walkthrough.limit: The model assumes one synthetic unit and simple direct allocation. Real programs need amortization, commitments, shared services, failed work, data-quality rules, and anti-gaming controls.

sources: AWS Well-Architected: define cost optimization KPIs
AWS cost allocation tags best practices
visual_explanation: The bars separate assigned teams from the unknown pool. The unit value changes with successful output; the dollar bar does not pretend that higher utilization costs less.
written_questions: Which denominator would be hardest for teams to game on your platform?
What allocation-coverage threshold would you require before chargeback?

title: Slice the eval before the average hides a dangerous failure
goal: Stratify agent evaluations so rare, high-risk tool cases cannot disappear inside an overall pass rate.
concept:
An average hospital wait time can look good while emergency patients wait dangerously long. Agent pass rates have the same trap. If 95 read-only cases pass and 5 payment cases fail, the overall score is still 95%.

Define important slices before running the eval: tool risk, customer tier, language, document length, or failure mode. Keep the total, but gate the release on critical slices too.
example: Candidate B passes 95/100 cases. The table reveals read-only tasks at 100% and payment tasks at 0%. A “≥90% overall” gate would ship it; a “≥90% overall and ≥80% payment” gate blocks it.

use_case.when: Use sliced evaluation whenever failures have unequal consequences or the production mix contains important minority cases.
use_case.example: Evaluate a support agent separately on read-only account lookup and money-moving refund tools.
use_case.decision: Predefine operationally meaningful slices and minimum sample sizes. Use the overall score for trend, but make high-risk slice thresholds independent release gates.

practice: Change the number of payment successes. Compare the overall bar with the payment slice gate.
boundary: This model uses deterministic binary labels and tiny synthetic slices. Real evals need representative sampling, grader validation, uncertainty, contamination checks, and manual review of consequential failures.
js:
function paintSlice(){const p=+paymentPass.value,read=95,overall=read+p,pct=20*p,ok=overall>=90&&pct>=80;sliceWorld.innerHTML='
Overall
'+overall+'%
Payments
'+pct+'%

Release gate: '+(ok?'PASS':'BLOCK')+' — both thresholds must pass.

';}paymentPass.oninput=paintSlice;paintSlice();
questions: Why can a 95% overall rate still be unsafe?
Rare critical cases may all fail
A majority slice can dominate the aggregate.
When should slice thresholds be chosen?
What if a critical slice has only two cases?
Treat it as weak evidence and add representative cases
Small samples cannot support a strong readiness claim.

steps.note: Separate the common and high-risk slices.
The aggregate looks strong because read-only cases dominate.
The critical slice reveals total failure.
Require both an overall and a risk-slice gate.

walkthrough.limit: This model uses deterministic binary labels and tiny synthetic slices. Real evals need representative sampling, grader validation, uncertainty, contamination checks, and manual review of consequential failures.

visual_explanation: The two bars share the same 0–100% scale. The release box combines them with AND, making it visually impossible for the large safe slice to erase the small risky slice.
written_questions: Which production slice would block your agent despite a strong overall score?
How would you detect that a grader is systematically lenient on one slice?

title: CXL memory pooling: lend capacity instead of stranding it
goal: Understand the promise and boundary of cache-coherent shared memory pools for uneven server demand.
concept:
Imagine four apartments, each keeping a private guest room “just in case.” Most rooms sit empty, while one apartment sometimes needs three. A shared guest floor could reduce stranded capacity.

CXL is a cache-coherent interconnect for processors, memory expansion, and accelerators. A memory pool can let hosts draw capacity through a fabric, but remote pooled memory has different latency, bandwidth, topology, failure, and software-management properties from local DIMMs.
example: Four hosts each own 128 GB but use 64, 80, 120, and 40 GB. That leaves 208 GB stranded in separate boxes. A 128 GB shared pool could cover a 64 GB burst for host 3 without installing 64 GB in every host.

use_case.when: Consider CXL memory expansion or pooling for fleets with uneven, expensive memory demand and software that can tolerate a different memory tier.
use_case.example: An inference fleet has bursty KV-cache demand; hosts borrow pooled capacity instead of reserving peak DRAM everywhere.
use_case.decision: Adopt only after benchmarking workload locality and validating fabric, NUMA, RAS, security, orchestration, and failure behavior. Local memory remains the safer latency baseline.

practice: Move one host’s burst. See whether fixed local memory fails and whether the pool covers it.
boundary: This is an arithmetic capacity model, not a CXL simulator or performance claim. It ignores fabric generations, latency, bandwidth, coherency traffic, switches, NUMA placement, security, operating-system support, and vendor implementation maturity.
js:
function paintCxl(){const b=+burstGb.value,localFree=8,pool=128,localOk=b<=localFree,poolOk=b<=localFree+pool;cxlWorld.innerHTML='
Host 3 local free
'+localFree+' GB
Local-only burst
'+(localOk?'fits':'short '+(b-localFree)+' GB')+'
CXL pool
'+pool+' GB shared
Pooled result
'+(poolOk?'capacity fits; benchmark latency':'pool exhausted')+'
';}burstGb.oninput=paintCxl;paintCxl();
questions: What problem does a memory pool mainly target?
A pool can shift capacity toward hosts that need it.
Does capacity fit prove performance fit?
No—latency, bandwidth, topology, and software still matter
Remote/tiered memory behavior must be measured.
What is the current public specification generation on the consortium page checked today?
The consortium page offers an evaluation copy of CXL 4.0 dated 2026.

steps.note: Model uneven memory use across four fixed hosts.
Unused local capacity totals 208 GB but cannot move by itself.
Host 3 has only 8 GB free before a 64 GB burst.
The pool solves the capacity arithmetic, not the performance proof.

walkthrough.limit: This is an arithmetic capacity model, not a CXL simulator or performance claim. It ignores fabric generations, latency, bandwidth, coherency traffic, switches, NUMA placement, security, operating-system support, and vendor implementation maturity.

sources: CXL 4.0 availability and feature summary; checked October 16, 2026
visual_explanation: The picture keeps local free memory, the failed local-only burst, and the shared pool separate. Green means capacity arithmetic works—not that latency or production readiness has been proven.

title: Give every matrix job its own artifact name
goal: Prevent immutable artifact-name collisions when parallel jobs upload results.
concept:
Four travelers cannot check four suitcases under one claim ticket and expect to retrieve the right bag. A matrix workflow has the same problem. Each job must upload to a unique artifact name.

With upload-artifact@v4, artifacts are immutable. Uploading multiple jobs to the same name is not a safe way to merge their files.
example: Linux and Windows jobs both upload test-results. The shared name collides. Use test-results-${{ matrix.os }}; a later aggregation job downloads each named artifact and combines reports explicitly.

use_case.when: Use matrix-qualified artifact names whenever parallel GitHub Actions jobs upload logs, binaries, coverage, or test reports.
use_case.example: Three operating-system jobs publish JUnit XML before one report job aggregates them.
use_case.decision: Treat each job output as immutable evidence. Name it with matrix dimensions and optionally run attempt; aggregate in a separate job rather than writing concurrently.

practice: Change the matrix size and naming policy. Watch duplicate names collapse into one collision group.
boundary: The browser does not run Actions or upload files. Real limits include retention, permissions, hidden files, compression, artifact IDs, action-version behavior, and naming constraints.

'+names.map((x,i)=>'
job '+(i+1)+'
'+x+'
').join('')+'

'+(distinct';}matrixJobs.oninput=paintArtifacts;uniqueNames.onchange=paintArtifacts;paintArtifacts();

Artifacts are immutable and parallel jobs collide
Each job should create its own artifact.

title: Budget GraphQL breadth before nested lists multiply
goal: Estimate nodes in a nested query, then paginate the level that drives growth.
concept:
Ordering “ten boxes, each with ten folders, each with ten pages” is not ten things—it is more than a thousand nodes. GraphQL lets clients choose shape, so nested list widths multiply.

Depth alone is not the whole problem. A shallow query with broad connections can still be expensive. Require pagination and apply node, point, time, or custom complexity limits.
example: A GitHub-style query asks for 10 repositories, 10 issues per repository, and 10 comments per issue: 10 repositories + 100 issues + 1,000 comments = 1,110 returned nodes, before other objects.

use_case.when: Use query-cost controls on GraphQL APIs that expose nested or expensive fields to varied clients.
use_case.example: A dashboard asks for repositories, issues, and comments in one request and can accidentally multiply work.
use_case.decision: Set field-aware budgets, require pagination on connections, and return a clear error before expensive execution. Prefer smaller pages for nested queries even when the maximum page size is higher.

practice: Change list widths. The visual calculates each layer and shows which pagination cut reduces the total most.
boundary: This arithmetic model treats every node equally. Real GraphQL cost depends on resolvers, caches, fan-out, authorization, database plans, federation, timeouts, and provider-specific formulas.
js:
function paintGql(){const r=+repoN.value,i=+issueN.value,c=+commentN.value,issues=r*i,comments=issues*c,total=r+issues+comments,budget=1000;gqlWorld.innerHTML='
Repositories
'+r+'
Issues
'+issues+'
Comments
'+comments+'

Total '+total+' · teaching budget '+budget+' · '+(total>budget?'reject or paginate':'within budget')+'

';}repoN.oninput=paintGql;issueN.oninput=paintGql;commentN.oninput=paintGql;paintGql();
questions: 10 repos × 10 issues × 10 comments produces how many comment nodes?
Why is a depth limit alone insufficient?
A shallow query can still request broad lists
Breadth can dominate even at modest depth.
What should the server do before executing an over-budget query?
Admission control should reject work before expensive fan-out.

steps.note: Set the width of each connection.
Issues multiply by repository count.
Comments multiply again.
The 1,110-node shape exceeds the synthetic budget.

walkthrough.limit: This arithmetic model treats every node equally. Real GraphQL cost depends on resolvers, caches, fan-out, authorization, database plans, federation, timeouts, and provider-specific formulas.

sources: GitHub GraphQL rate and query limits
visual_explanation: The bars are counts by layer, not latency claims. The comments bar grows from both parent widths, making the multiplicative source visible rather than drawing a generic request arrow.
written_questions: Which fields in your schema need higher complexity weights than a plain node count?
What partial-data behavior should a client expect after a cost rejection?
